cases.holding: The division held that the Child Protection Act and the Colorado Governmental Immunity Act can be read together, so that a public-employee mandatory reporter is immune from liability for reporting or failing to report child abuse unless the conduct was willful and wanton, and remanded for a Trinity hearing on that question.
cases.quote: persons who report child abuse under section 19-3-304 are immune from liability unless their conduct is willful, wanton, and malicious.

relevance.INP-01: This is the controlling Colorado statement of the scope and limits of mandatory-reporter immunity under C.R.S. § 19-3-309, which is what makes the reporting duty at this node enforceable without exposing the reporter to suit.
relevance.INP-02: The immunity in § 19-3-309 runs to 'any person' participating in good faith in making a report, not only to listed professionals, which is the protection a voluntary third-party reporter relies on.
relevance.INP-06: A hotline or anonymous caller acting in good faith is within the 'any person' immunity the division construed here, and loses it only on willful, wanton and malicious conduct.
relevance.INP-07: Physicians and other health-care mandatory reporters listed in § 19-3-304(2) are the 'persons' whose immunity this opinion defines.
relevance.INP-08: Public and private school employees are express § 19-3-304(2) reporters, and this case fixes both their immunity and the willful-and-wanton exception that a family could plead against them.
relevance.DEC-02: Because immunity falls away only for willful, wanton and malicious conduct, the opinion sets the practical liability floor for the agency and law-enforcement conduct that follows acceptance of a report.
relevance.DEC-03: The division treats the reporting and investigation chain in article 3 as a single statutory scheme, which is the framework in which a substantiated finding is later attacked.
relevance.PMC-03: The opinion's reading of the Child Protection Act as a coordinated scheme of duties and immunities is the state-law baseline against which citizen-review oversight of reporting practice has to be measured.

cases.case_name: Berges v. County Court of Douglas County
cases.holding: The division held that section 19-3-206's grant of exclusive authority to county attorneys over article 3 proceedings does not strip district attorneys of their authority to criminally prosecute mandatory reporters who willfully fail to report under section 19-3-304.
cases.quote: section 19-3-304 does not set forth a proceeding under article 3; it simply defines an offense.

relevance.INP-01: This case establishes that a mandatory reporter's willful failure to report is a criminal misdemeanor prosecutable by the district attorney, which is the enforcement mechanism behind the reporting duty at this node.
relevance.INP-02: It marks the line between the reporting duty that carries criminal sanction (listed reporters) and the permissive reporting available to anyone else.
relevance.INP-07: The prosecutions at issue arose from health-care and institutional personnel; the opinion confirms who may charge them for a willful failure to report a medical disclosure.
relevance.INP-08: School officials are among the reporters the division identified as subject to misdemeanor prosecution for willfully violating the reporting duty.

cases.case_name: Wilson v. State Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The division reversed, holding that the central registry director could not amend a confirmed child-abuse report without good cause and prior notice to the subject, that the amended reports had to be expunged, and that findings resting on an uncharged incident violated the subject's procedural due process rights.
cases.quote: the statute requires that notice of a proposed amendment be given so that the subject of the report may dispute the existence of "good cause" for that amendment.

relevance.INP-01: The registry entry that follows a reporter's call is what this case regulates: the subject must be told the child's name, type of abuse and date of incident within 60 days.
relevance.INP-02: A report from any source that is confirmed reaches the central registry, and this opinion fixes the notice a subject is owed once it does.
relevance.INP-06: Reports originating from the hotline end in the same central registry record whose notice and amendment rules the division enforced here.
relevance.INP-10: The opinion describes the statutory path from report to county investigation to a confirmed registry entry, which is the escalation sequence this node captures.
relevance.DEC-01: Because the subject may petition to amend, seal or expunge within two years, the case supplies the due-process route for contesting a report that should have been closed out.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the leading published Colorado decision on the procedural due process owed to a person named in a substantiated (confirmed) child-abuse finding.
relevance.FAIL-01: The court reversed the agency's refusal to expunge and ordered relief, an example of judicial correction of an agency finding made without required notice.
relevance.FAIL-06: The department's failure to send the statutory notice of the registry listing is itself the disclosure failure that vitiated the proceeding.
relevance.PMC-05: The notice content mandated by § 19-3-313(6)(a) is a statutory transparency duty owed directly to the individual, enforceable on review.

cases.holding: The court held that the Department of Human Services failed to carry its burden of showing that the Children's Records Act confidentiality provision barred release, and ordered disclosure of the aggregate number of child-abuse reports and screened-in reports from three named residential child care facilities.
cases.quote: we conclude that CDHS must disclose the six cardinal numbers requested by the Media Organizations.

relevance.INP-06: The counts the court ordered released are precisely the hotline-report totals for named facilities, showing that aggregate intake data is not shielded by the informant-address exception.
relevance.INP-09: This is the current Colorado authority letting press and public obtain the intake and screening data that oversight of a facility or county depends on.
relevance.INP-10: The requested figures included the number of reports screened in for investigation, so the case directly governs public access to escalation statistics.
relevance.DEC-01: Screened-out versus screened-in counts are the very records ordered disclosed, which makes agency screening decisions auditable from outside.
relevance.DEC-03: The custodian bears the burden of showing a confidentiality exception applies before withholding data about reports and their disposition.
relevance.OUT-06: The dispute arose from reporting on harm to children in residential child care facilities; the ruling keeps that data public.
relevance.FAIL-04: Aggregate abuse-report data from facilities housing children in state care is disclosable, which is the record base for detecting deaths and serious harm in care.
relevance.FAIL-06: This is the leading recent Colorado decision holding an agency to its burden when it refuses to disclose child-welfare records.
relevance.PMC-02: The opinion confirms that financial and operational auditing of child-welfare providers can rest on records the department must release.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review of CPS policy requires the screening and report data the court ordered produced.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality and serious-harm review of facility care depends on the facility-level report counts the court held disclosable.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the controlling Colorado open-records holding for child-welfare data requests.
relevance.PMC-06: Any cross-jurisdiction data analysis of Colorado intake and screening rests on the disclosure obligation the court enforced here.

cases.case_name: H.B. v. Lake County District Court
cases.holding: The court held that the district attorney is not authorized to prosecute dependency and neglect proceedings under article 3, and remanded with directions to order the recusal of the district attorney's office, which was simultaneously prosecuting the related criminal case.
cases.quote: we conclude that the district attorney is not authorized to prosecute article 3 proceedings.

relevance.INP-03: When law enforcement and the district attorney are already pursuing a criminal case, this decision separates that role from the civil child-protection case that the referral generates.
relevance.INP-04: It fixes who may appear for the petitioner once a court or agency sets an article 3 case in motion: the county attorney, not the district attorney.
relevance.DEC-05: This is the controlling Colorado authority on who is authorized to file and prosecute a dependency or neglect petition.
relevance.FAIL-06: The conflict identified turned on section 19-3-207's limits on using information across the civil and criminal tracks, a core confidentiality boundary in Colorado practice.

cases.holding: The court held that a juvenile court exceeds its jurisdiction if it transfers legal custody of a child from a parent to the county department at a pre-adjudicatory shelter hearing; at that stage the court may only continue shelter or release the child, and a temporary protective custody order reaches physical custody only.
cases.quote: We will not infer from statutory silence a jurisdictional grant to a juvenile court to sever legal custody from a natural parent at a pre-adjudicatory shelter hearing.

relevance.INP-04: It defines exactly what a juvenile court may and may not order before adjudication when a case is opened on referral.
relevance.INP-05: A parent who seeks help voluntarily is protected by the rule that legal custody cannot be taken without adjudication and a dispositional decree.
relevance.INP-12: This is the leading Colorado case on the limits of emergency protective custody: 72 hours maximum, physical custody only, with a shelter hearing within 48 hours.
relevance.DEC-04: The decision confines an emergency removal decision to physical custody pending adjudication and bars any de facto dispositional order at the shelter stage.
relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement pending adjudication is a placement order only; legal custody may be vested elsewhere only after an adjudication under section 19-3-111.
relevance.ACT-05: The opinion catalogues the pre-adjudicatory protective orders a juvenile court may issue and distinguishes them from custody transfers.
relevance.ACT-06: The court explains that the shelter statute separately authorizes emergency medical care for a sheltered child when the parents are not immediately available, which is why no custody transfer is needed for that purpose.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal order that strips legal custody before adjudication is in excess of jurisdiction and therefore unlawful under Colorado law.

cases.holding: The court held that the juvenile court had jurisdiction under the Children's Code to take the case at a shelter hearing and to issue temporary orders providing for the medical treatment of a gravely injured child whose parents were unable and unavailable to act, and that its order was proper.
cases.quote: We hold, therefore, that the court had jurisdiction and its action was proper.

relevance.INP-04: The case shows the juvenile court exercising jurisdiction and ordering protective and medical measures at the outset of a child-protection matter.
relevance.INP-05: Where a parent is unavailable or unable to act, the Children's Code supplies the court, not the parent, as the decision-maker for the child's care.
relevance.INP-07: The matter reached the court through a hospital and treating physicians, the classic medical-disclosure pathway into child protection.
relevance.ACT-05: Section 19-1-104 authorizes temporary orders for protection and support before adjudication, the statutory source of protective orders at this node.
relevance.ACT-06: This is the leading Colorado authority that a juvenile court may order emergency and extraordinary medical treatment for a child before its jurisdiction is adjudicated.
relevance.FAIL-04: The case arose from catastrophic abuse-caused injury and shows the judicial machinery available when a child in the system is dying.

cases.holding: Following Santosky, the court held that due process requires the grounds for terminating parental rights to be proved by clear and convincing evidence, while the predicate adjudication of dependency or neglect may constitutionally rest on a preponderance of the evidence; the termination order was reversed and a new trial ordered.
cases.quote: we hold that clear and convincing evidence is the appropriate constitutional standard of proof in proceedings involving termination of a parent-child relationship.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the foundational Colorado decision setting the constitutional burden of proof for termination of parental rights and is still the case every later Colorado termination opinion builds on.
relevance.PMC-06: The Mathews v. Eldridge balancing the court performed is the analytic template Colorado courts still use to test whether a child-welfare procedure is fundamentally fair.

cases.holding: The court held that neither the injurious-environment provision of section 19-3-102(1)(c) nor Troxel requires the State to prove parental fault, or to prove that both parents lack the availability, ability and willingness to provide reasonable parental care, before a child may be adjudicated dependent or neglected.
cases.quote: We hold that the statute does not require the jury to make findings of parental fault

relevance.DEC-05: This is the controlling Colorado statement of what the State must prove to obtain an adjudication after a petition is filed, and of what it need not prove.
relevance.OUT-05: It marks the boundary of the adjudication: a case is not dismissible merely because one parent is fit or because no parent is at fault.

cases.case_name: People in Interest of S.N. v. S.N.
cases.holding: The court held that whether a child is dependent and neglected because of prospective harm is a mixed question of law and fact, so summary judgment in such adjudications is neither always available nor always barred and must be evaluated case by case on whether the material evidentiary facts are undisputed.
cases.quote: We hold that courts must evaluate whether summary judgment is appropriate in a dependency and neglect adjudication involving prospective harm on a case-by-case basis.

relevance.INP-10: The prospective-harm theory is what allows a screened report about future risk to be escalated into an adjudicable case.
relevance.DEC-01: The opinion identifies what evidentiary material actually has to be in dispute, which is the test for whether a risk-based report can be closed out or must proceed.
relevance.DEC-05: It governs how a prospective-harm dependency petition may be resolved short of trial.
relevance.OUT-05: A parent contesting an adjudication has the right to a factual hearing unless the material evidentiary facts are genuinely undisputed, which is the route to dismissal at this node.

cases.holding: The court held that the State's burden at a dispositional hearing on whether an appropriate treatment plan can be devised is preponderance of the evidence, and that proof of a single incident resulting in serious bodily injury to the child suffices to support a no-appropriate-treatment-plan finding without proof that the parent caused the injury.
cases.quote: we conclude the district court erred by imposing a clear and convincing burden of proof on the state at the dispositional hearing.

relevance.DEC-05: The opinion sets the proof standard that governs the dispositional stage immediately following the petition and adjudication.
relevance.DEC-06: It defines the statutory circumstance in which the no-treatment-plan route displaces any service-based alternative response.
relevance.ACT-01: Where a single serious-bodily-injury incident is shown, the court may find that no appropriate plan can be devised, which forecloses the voluntary-services path.
relevance.ACT-02: This is the controlling Colorado authority on when a court must adopt a treatment plan and when it may find that none can be devised.
relevance.OUT-06: The holding turns on the statutory category of a single incident causing serious bodily injury, which is the serious-injury trigger at this node.
relevance.FAIL-04: The case shows the dispositional consequence Colorado attaches to serious bodily injury to a child already before the court.

cases.holding: The court held that section 19-1-109(1) authorizes an appeal from any final order in a dependency or neglect proceeding, that subsection (2) adds to rather than limits that right, and that C.A.R. 3.4(a) cannot narrow the categories of orders the statute makes appealable.
cases.quote: we hold that section 19-1-109(1) authorizes the appeal of any order from a dependency or neglect proceeding that is "final"

relevance.INP-04: Orders entered when a court sets a child-protection case in motion are reviewable if final, which is the check on judicially initiated involvement.
relevance.INP-09: Appellate review under section 19-1-109 is the principal case-level oversight mechanism in Colorado dependency practice.
relevance.DEC-05: Orders disposing of a petition as to a party are appealable when final, which matters immediately after filing.
relevance.OUT-04: Because the statute governs appeals from any final order, it is the vehicle for challenging orders about a youth's continued placement and the court's continuing jurisdiction.
relevance.OUT-05: An order dismissing a respondent or the petition is reviewable if final.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the Colorado Supreme Court's statement of the appellate jurisdiction through which agency and trial-court errors in dependency cases are corrected.
relevance.PMC-06: Systemic analysis of Colorado dependency outcomes depends on this holding, which keeps the full range of final dependency orders within appellate review.

cases.holding: The court held that consideration of less drastic alternatives is implicit in the statutory termination criteria, that due process does not require express findings on them, and that the child's best interests rather than an 'adequacy' standard control; it reversed the court of appeals for substituting its judgment for the trial court's.
cases.quote: Implicit in these criteria is the requirement that the trial court consider and eliminate less drastic alternatives.

relevance.ACT-02: The court restates the four statutory findings, including non-compliance with or failure of an appropriate court-approved treatment plan, that a service order must be measured against.
relevance.ACT-04: The less drastic alternative litigated was permanent custody to the child's paternal aunt, which is the kinship option courts must consider before termination.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification and other non-termination outcomes are evaluated as less drastic alternatives, but only if they serve the child's best interests.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the current controlling Colorado authority on less drastic alternatives and the best-interests standard in termination.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanent custody or guardianship with a relative is a recognized less drastic alternative that must be weighed against the child's best interests.
relevance.FAIL-01: The court of appeals had reversed a termination, and the Supreme Court held that reversal improperly substituted appellate judgment for the trial court's factual findings.

cases.holding: The court held that foster parents who satisfy the criteria of section 19-3-507(5)(a) may intervene and participate fully as parties at a termination hearing, and that parents' due process rights are not impaired by that full participation.
cases.quote: Foster parent intervenors are afforded the same degree of participation as all other parties, and such participation is not limited to the dispositional hearing.

relevance.ACT-03: Once a child has been in a foster home for more than three months, the foster parents acquire a statutory right to intervene as parties, which changes the litigation posture of the placement.

cases.holding: The court held that the father impliedly waived his statutory right to appointed counsel through obstructive and dilatory conduct and that the district court did not abuse its discretion in finding no less drastic alternative to termination, but vacated the termination order because the court may have lacked UCCJEA jurisdiction to modify an out-of-state custody determination.
cases.quote: we conclude that the district court did not violate father's statutory right to appointed counsel because father had impliedly waived it through his obstreperous and dilatory conduct.

relevance.OUT-01: The opinion addresses the department's reasonable efforts to reunite the family and the jurisdictional prerequisites that must exist before a Colorado court can alter an out-of-state custody arrangement.

cases.holding: The court held that ICWA's 'active efforts' standard is heightened and more demanding than 'reasonable efforts,' requiring affirmative, active, thorough and timely remedial services tailored to the case, though the agency retains discretion to prioritize services, and it overruled People ex rel. K.D. to the extent inconsistent.
cases.quote: the active efforts standard under ICWA is a more demanding standard than the reasonable efforts standard applied in non-ICWA cases.

relevance.INP-11: This is the controlling Colorado authority on what ICWA requires of a county department once a child is identified as an Indian child.
relevance.OUT-01: Where ICWA applies, reunification efforts are measured against the heightened active-efforts standard, not the ordinary reasonable-efforts standard.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to meet ICWA's active-efforts requirement is a federal-law compliance failure that Colorado courts will enforce against the agency.
relevance.PMC-01: Active efforts is a federal performance standard that state agency practice is measured against, of the same kind CFSR monitoring reviews.

cases.holding: The division held that 25 U.S.C. § 1912(f) requires a beyond-a-reasonable-doubt determination of likely serious emotional or physical damage supported by qualified expert testimony, but that the expert need not recite the statutory language, and affirmed the termination.
cases.quote: the trial court's determination must be supported by evidence that includes testimony from qualified expert witnesses.

relevance.INP-11: This decision fixes the qualified-expert-witness requirement that attaches once a case is identified as involving an Indian child.
relevance.OUT-02: Termination of parental rights to an Indian child in Colorado requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt supported by qualified expert testimony, a higher bar than the ordinary clear and convincing standard.

cases.holding: The division held that section 19-1-126(1)(a) required the department to make new ICWA inquiries in this case, and that findings and orders from a sibling's earlier case could not alone support a determination that ICWA did not apply; the judgment was reversed and the case remanded.
cases.quote: we conclude that the findings and orders from the prior case alone are insufficient to support the trial court's conclusion that ICWA does not apply in this case.

relevance.INP-11: This is the Colorado authority on the continuing duty of inquiry that triggers ICWA at the front end of every new case, even for a sibling of a child already screened.
relevance.FAIL-01: The court reversed a termination judgment outright for the department's and trial court's failure to conduct the statutory ICWA inquiry.
relevance.FAIL-03: Skipping the ICWA inquiry required by state and federal law is a compliance failure serious enough to void the resulting judgment.

cases.holding: As a matter of first impression the division held that the Americans with Disabilities Act does not pre-empt section 19-3-604(1)(b)(I), because the question whether reasonable accommodations could address a parent's mental impairment is subsumed within the statutory question whether an appropriate treatment plan can be devised.
cases.quote: we conclude that it does not conflict with the ADA's requirement that a public entity make reasonable accommodations for qualified individuals with disabilities.

relevance.DEC-06: Where a parent's unfitness stems from mental impairment that no accommodation can address, the statute permits proceeding without the service-based route this node describes.
relevance.ACT-01: The decision explains when the department is and is not obliged to offer rehabilitative services to a parent with a disability before seeking termination.
relevance.ACT-02: It defines the relationship between the ADA accommodation duty and the court's determination that no appropriate treatment plan can be devised.
relevance.FAIL-05: This is the leading Colorado decision on disability discrimination claims in child-welfare proceedings, and it encourages trial courts to make express accommodation findings.

cases.holding: The division held that a juvenile court must consider reasonable accommodations for a parent's disability in deciding whether the treatment plan was appropriate and whether the department made reasonable efforts to rehabilitate the parent, and affirmed because the court had done so.
cases.quote: a juvenile court must consider reasonable accommodations in deciding whether such a parent's treatment plan was appropriate and whether reasonable efforts were made to rehabilitate the parent.

relevance.DEC-06: Whether services can be delivered with accommodation bears directly on whether a family can be served without escalation.
relevance.ACT-01: Accommodation must be built into the services offered to a disabled parent from the outset, not raised only at termination.
relevance.ACT-02: This is the Colorado rule that a court-ordered treatment plan is appropriate only if it accounts for reasonable accommodations for the parent's disability.
relevance.OUT-01: Reasonable efforts toward reunification are measured with accommodation for a parent's disability built in.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to accommodate is assessed as part of the reasonable-efforts determination that federal Title IV-E funding depends on.
relevance.FAIL-05: This decision supplies the operative Colorado test for disability-based discrimination claims against a county department in a dependency case.
relevance.PMC-01: Reasonable efforts is the federal performance measure at the center of CFSR review, and this case states how Colorado courts apply it.

cases.holding: The division held that a county department may not seek involuntary termination through an article 5 relinquishment proceeding while an article 3 dependency and neglect case is open, because the dependency court retains continuing exclusive jurisdiction over the child's status until majority or until that jurisdiction is otherwise terminated.
cases.quote: the dependency and neglect court maintains continuing, exclusive jurisdiction over any child who has been adjudicated dependent and neglected.

relevance.INP-05: A parent's voluntary relinquishment route cannot be used to bypass the open dependency case, which is where a guardian's request for help is handled.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanency, including relinquishment and adoption, must be achieved within the dependency court's continuing exclusive jurisdiction rather than in a parallel case.
relevance.OUT-04: This is the clearest published Colorado statement of how long the dependency court's jurisdiction over an adjudicated child runs, which is the framework for continued placement as a youth approaches majority.

cases.holding: The division held that foster parent intervenors have standing to appeal an order denying a motion to terminate parental rights, and affirmed the denial because the trial court applied the correct legal standard and its findings were supported by the record.
cases.quote: we conclude that the Intervenors have standing to appeal a decision in a termination proceeding.

relevance.ACT-04: Caregivers who have had the child in their home long enough to intervene obtain full party rights, including the right to appeal, which is the procedural leverage a kin or foster caregiver has.
relevance.OUT-03: A caregiver seeking permanency can carry the issue to the court of appeals in her own right.
relevance.OUT-05: The case is the Colorado authority on appellate review of an order denying termination and leaving the case on a reunification track.

cases.holding: The division held that a grandparent who enjoys only statutory visitation rights and has a biological but no existing custodial relationship with the child has no constitutionally protected liberty interest in the child's society or custody, and was therefore not entitled to notice of the termination hearing.
cases.quote: To establish a due process violation, an individual must show that he or she has a protected liberty interest.

relevance.ACT-04: This is the Colorado decision defining what a relative must have — an existing custodial relationship, not mere biology — before constitutional protections attach to a kinship placement claim.
relevance.OUT-03: A grandparent seeking permanency has statutory, not constitutional, standing, which determines what notice and hearing rights she can demand.

cases.case_name: Malik v. Arapahoe County Department of Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that procuring an ex parte child custody order through distortion, misrepresentation and omission, and in retaliation for a parent's retaining counsel, violated clearly established Fourth, First and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
cases.quote: it was clearly established law that, except in extraordinary circumstances, a parent has a liberty interest in familial association and privacy that cannot be violated without adequate pre-deprivation procedures.

relevance.INP-03: The opinion holds that law enforcement and caseworkers may seek protective custody where they genuinely believe the child is in danger, but not to circumvent a lawyer's attempt to negotiate interview conditions.
relevance.INP-12: It reads C.R.S. § 19-3-405(2)(a) as permitting temporary protective custody only on a belief that remaining would endanger the child's life or health in the reasonably foreseeable future.
relevance.DEC-02: Retaliating against a parent for retaining counsel during an investigation independently violates the First Amendment under DeLoach.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the leading Tenth Circuit case arising from Colorado on what makes an ex parte emergency custody order constitutionally defective.
relevance.FAIL-02: An ex parte hearing procured by misrepresentation and omission is not notice and an opportunity to be heard, which is the core of an unlawful-removal claim in this circuit.
relevance.FAIL-05: Retaliation against a parent for exercising the right to counsel is actionable under section 1983 as a First Amendment violation.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit adopted a reasonable-suspicion standard for warrantless emergency removal, holding that officials may remove a child without prior notice and hearing only on reasonable suspicion of an immediate threat to the child's safety and must then provide a prompt post-removal hearing, and found the defendants entitled to qualified immunity on these facts.
cases.quote: even in these instances in which emergency removal is justified, the state must afford the parents a prompt post-removal hearing.

relevance.INP-12: This is the governing Tenth Circuit standard for taking a child into protective custody without a court order.
relevance.DEC-04: The court also requires consideration of whether officials could have obtained judicial authorization without additional risk, so that 'emergency' is not defined so broadly that due process erodes.
relevance.ACT-03: A placement made on emergency authority must be promptly ratified in a post-removal hearing before it can continue.
relevance.FAIL-02: Removal without reasonable suspicion of an immediate threat, or without a prompt post-removal hearing, is the constitutional violation this node describes.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed dismissal on qualified immunity, holding that although an El Paso County caseworker's warrantless visual inspection and photographing of a four-year-old's unclothed body at school was a search conducted without a warrant, consent or exigency, it was not clearly established that the special needs doctrine could not justify it.
cases.quote: Ms. Woodard needed a warrant or one of the exceptions to the warrant requirement to apply—consent, exigent circumstances, or the special needs doctrine.

relevance.INP-08: The search took place at the child's school after an abuse report, the precise setting in which school-based disclosures are investigated.
relevance.DEC-02: This is the controlling Tenth Circuit framework for whether a caseworker's investigative examination of a child requires a warrant, consent or exigency.
relevance.FAIL-02: The opinion identifies the constitutional limits on caseworker searches of children while recognizing that qualified immunity may still defeat damages where the law was unsettled.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit reversed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that the plaintiff had not shown clearly established law creating a special relationship between himself and the Colorado adoption-exchange officials who arranged his out-of-state placement, and declined to decide whether the special-relationship doctrine can cross state lines.
cases.quote: First, the plaintiff must demonstrate the existence of a special relationship, meaning that the plaintiff completely depended on the state to satisfy basic human needs.

relevance.ACT-03: Once the state takes custody and places a child, the special-relationship doctrine is the source of the state's affirmative constitutional duty to protect that child.
relevance.OUT-06: This is the Tenth Circuit's statement of the four elements a foster child or estate must plead when serious harm or death occurs in state-arranged care.
relevance.FAIL-04: It defines both the availability and the limits of section 1983 liability for officials whose failure to protect results in harm to a child under agency supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality and serious-harm review depends on knowing which officials owed a constitutional duty, which is what the special-relationship inquiry determines.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit reversed a grant of qualified immunity, holding that the alleged coercive detention of a teenager at school by a social services official and a deputy, to compel her to change her residence, stated a violation of her clearly established Fourth Amendment right to be free from unreasonable seizure.
cases.quote: the prohibition against unreasonable seizures extends to civil, as well as criminal, investigations by the government.

relevance.INP-03: The seizure was carried out jointly by a child welfare official and a deputy sheriff, the classic joint-response posture at this node.
relevance.INP-10: Escalating a case by compelling a child's attendance and compliance is itself state action measured by the Fourth Amendment.
relevance.INP-12: Taking physical control of a child outside the home is a seizure that must be justified, not an administrative act.
relevance.DEC-02: Investigative contact with a child can become a Fourth Amendment seizure, which constrains how an accepted report may be worked.
relevance.FAIL-02: The case establishes that children seized by child-welfare officials without justification have a section 1983 remedy in this circuit.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may sever parental rights, due process requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence, and struck down New York's fair-preponderance standard, leaving to the States any higher burden.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal constitutional floor for termination of parental rights that Colorado adopted in People in Interest of A.M.D. and still applies.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that there is no categorical due process right to appointed counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings; the decision is made case by case by the trial court subject to appellate review, and no error occurred on these facts.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding.

relevance.OUT-02: Lassiter is the federal floor for counsel in termination cases; Colorado exceeds it by statute, which is why B.H. analyses waiver of a statutory rather than a constitutional right.

cases.holding: The court held that coroners' autopsy reports are public records open to inspection under the Colorado Open Records Act, that a requester need not show a special interest to obtain them, and that a custodian who denies access must state the legal ground and may seek a protective order from the district court.
cases.quote: This statement of policy clearly eliminates any requirement that a person seeking access to public records show a special interest in those records in order to be permitted access thereto.

relevance.INP-09: Public access to death-investigation records without any showing of special interest is the evidentiary basis on which outside oversight of a fatality begins.
relevance.OUT-06: Autopsy reports on a child who dies are public records, which is the principal documentary route to understanding a fatality in or near agency care.
relevance.FAIL-06: The case sets the default of openness and puts the burden on the custodian to identify a statutory exception or seek a court order.
relevance.PMC-02: It establishes the general CORA presumption of access that financial and program audits of public agencies depend on.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality review work in Colorado is built on the public status of coroners' autopsy reports confirmed here.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the foundational Colorado Open Records Act holding on the public's right of inspection and the procedure when a custodian denies it.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination, holding that a trial court's consideration and elimination of alternatives less drastic than termination is implicit in the statutory termination criteria, so that no separate express finding is required, and that a treatment plan's appropriateness is measured against the realities that produced the dependency adjudication rather than by whether it ultimately succeeded.
cases.quote: adherence to the statutory criteria for termination requires a trial court to consider less drastic alternatives and to reject those alternatives as unavailing before entering an order of termination

relevance.ACT-02: This is the foundational Colorado holding on what makes a court-ordered treatment plan appropriate — a plan reasonably calculated to render this parent fit within a reasonable time, measured against the conditions that caused the adjudication — and it is the source A.M., 2021 CO 14, cites for the less-drastic-alternatives rule.
relevance.OUT-01: The court explains that the purpose of a treatment plan is to preserve the parent-child relationship wherever possible by helping the parent overcome the problems that led to the dependency adjudication, which is the reunification premise of the whole scheme.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanent foster care was the less drastic permanency alternative the trial court expressly considered and rejected on the record, which is how a non-termination permanency option must be handled before rights are severed.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination of the mother's parental rights, holding that ample evidence supported the district court's findings under the section 19-3-604(1)(c) criteria — failure of an appropriate treatment plan, unfitness, and conduct unlikely to change within a reasonable time — and restating that a court ruling on a termination motion must give primary consideration to the child's physical, mental and emotional conditions and needs.
cases.quote: In considering a motion to terminate the parent-child legal relationship, the court shall give primary consideration to the physical, mental, and emotional conditions and needs of the child.

relevance.ACT-02: This is the current Colorado Supreme Court statement of the section 19-3-604(1)(c) criteria against which a court-ordered treatment plan is measured, including the expedited-permanency rule that a parent who exhibits the same problems without adequate improvement cannot be found in reasonable compliance.

cases.holding: The court reversed the court of appeals and upheld the termination order, holding that the division failed to apply the clearly erroneous standard and improperly substituted its own view of witness credibility and of the weight, sufficiency and probative value of the evidence for the trial court's.
cases.quote: we set aside a trial court's factual findings only when they are "so clearly erroneous as to find no support in the record."

relevance.OUT-02: This is the governing Colorado authority on the deference an appellate court owes a trial court's unfitness, change-of-condition and best-interests findings in a termination case, and it is what A.M., 2021 CO 14, relies on for that rule.
relevance.FAIL-01: It marks the outer limit of judicial correction of a termination: a reviewing court may not reverse by reweighing credibility and evidence that the record in fact supports.

cases.holding: The division affirmed the denial of a maternal aunt's motion to intervene, holding that an extended family member with no existing custodial relationship has no constitutionally protected liberty interest in the child's society or custody and so is not entitled to notice of the termination hearing, but vacated the portion of the order treating timely intervention as a precondition to being considered as an adoptive parent.
cases.quote: the failure of § 19-3-605 to require that she, as an extended family member, be notified of the termination hearing does not constitute a procedural due process violation

relevance.ACT-04: This is the source decision holding that a relative must have an existing custodial relationship, not mere kinship, before constitutional protections attach to a kinship placement claim — the rule People in Interest of C.N. later follows and applies.
relevance.OUT-03: A relative seeking permanency must file her request for custody under section 19-3-605 before the termination hearing begins, and the division confirmed that failing to intervene does not disqualify her from later being considered as an adoptive parent.

cases.holding: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding that UCCJEA temporary emergency jurisdiction is limited to abandoned children and to emergencies of mistreatment or abuse, that the juvenile court therefore lacked that jurisdiction when it terminated parental rights and the termination judgment was properly vacated, but that the division erred in directing contact with an Arkansas court without first analysing whether Arkansas had home-state jurisdiction on the date of the termination order.
cases.quote: we hold that UCCJEA temporary emergency jurisdiction exists only to protect abandoned children or to prevent mistreatment or abuse in emergencies

relevance.INP-12: Emergency jurisdiction over a child present in Colorado but belonging to another state's courts exists only for abandonment or an actual ongoing emergency of mistreatment or abuse, which bounds the state's authority when it takes such a child into protective custody.
relevance.OUT-01: This is the companion decision to People in Interest of B.H., issued the same day, and it supplies the jurisdictional analysis a Colorado court must complete before it may displace an out-of-state custody arrangement rather than continue working the case toward reunification.
relevance.OUT-04: Continuing authority over a youth's placement depends on a UCCJEA jurisdictional basis that exists at the time each order is entered, not merely at the time the case was opened.

cases.case_name: Trinity Broadcasting of Denver, Inc. v. City of Westminster
cases.holding: The court reversed the summary judgment on the Governmental Immunity Act notice issue and remanded, holding that a pretrial governmental-immunity challenge is a jurisdictional question for the trial court under C.R.C.P. 12(b)(1), on which the court may permit limited discovery and must hold an evidentiary hearing when the jurisdictional facts are disputed, rather than resolving it on summary judgment or reserving it for the jury.
cases.quote: When a public entity claims before trial that timely notice was not given to it under the Governmental Immunity Act, the trial court is the finder of fact.

relevance.INP-01: This is the decision that supplies the procedure — the 'Trinity hearing' — a trial court must use to resolve a mandatory reporter's or agency employee's Governmental Immunity Act defence, which is exactly what L.J. v. Carricato ordered on remand.
relevance.DEC-02: Any state-law tort claim arising from how an accepted report was investigated must clear this jurisdictional procedure, decided by the judge on evidence, before it can reach a jury.

cases.holding: The court reversed and remanded, holding that a public employee who asserts that his conduct was not willful and wanton under section 24-10-118(2)(a) is claiming sovereign immunity and may appeal its denial, that the trial court must resolve all issues bearing on that immunity claim including factual ones at a Trinity hearing rather than merely test the pleadings, and that willful and wanton conduct requires conscious disregard of the danger rather than negligence.
cases.quote: willful and wanton conduct is not merely negligent; instead, it must exhibit a conscious disregard for the danger.

relevance.INP-01: It supplies the substantive standard and the procedure for the willful-and-wanton exception that strips a public-employee mandatory reporter of Governmental Immunity Act immunity under the rule stated in L.J. v. Carricato.
relevance.DEC-02: A caseworker or officer sued in tort over the handling of an accepted report keeps immunity unless the plaintiff proves conscious disregard of the danger, and the trial court, not a jury, must decide that question before trial.
relevance.FAIL-04: A state-law damages claim arising from a child's death or serious injury under agency supervision must satisfy this willful-and-wanton standard, resolved by the court at a Trinity hearing.

cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of the CORA complaint, holding that where the custodian is an individual who is also a public official the requester must first allege facts showing the record was made, maintained or kept in an official capacity before the burden shifts to the official, and that the Governor's personal cell phone bills, kept only to pay them, were not shown to be likely public records.
cases.quote: When the custodian of a requested record is an individual who is also a public official, the plaintiff must show that the record is likely a public record.

relevance.INP-09: Outside oversight that begins with a records request must carry this threshold showing before a custodian is put to the burden of justifying a withholding.
relevance.PMC-02: Financial and program auditing through CORA reaches records made, maintained or kept in an official capacity, and this opinion draws that boundary under the current statute.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the modern Colorado Supreme Court decision applying the current sections 24-72-201 to -206 text and allocating the burdens between requester and custodian, which Dreyfus (1974) predates.
relevance.FAIL-06: A refusal to produce is not automatically a transparency failure: the requester must plead facts showing the material is likely a public record before the agency must justify withholding it.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the invalidation of a nonparental visitation order, holding that the Washington statute as applied violated the mother's due process right to make decisions concerning the care, custody and control of her children because the trial court gave no special weight to the presumption that a fit parent acts in her children's best interests.
cases.quote: there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children

relevance.INP-05: Where a parent or guardian asks the agency for help and has never been found unfit, this presumption limits what the state may impose in exchange for that help.
relevance.ACT-01: Colorado has no published appellate decision construing voluntary service agreements, so this is the federal constitutional baseline for the node: services accepted without an adjudication cannot be used to override a fit parent's decisions about her children.
relevance.DEC-06: An alternative-response track that avoids a petition also avoids any adjudication of unfitness, so the agency's leverage over the family is bounded by the presumption the Court states here.

IMPORTANT SUPERSESSION: the Colorado Court of Appeals decision in Colorado Sun v. Brubaker, 2023 COA 101, 542 P.3d 1190 (cluster 9439106) was retrieved and read, but it was REVERSED by the Colorado Supreme Court in Brubaker v. Colorado Sun, 2026 CO 18 (Mar. 30, 2026). The supreme court did not adopt the division's ambiguity/legislative-history reading of C.R.S. section 19-1-307(1)(a); it applied the plain meaning and held that CDHS had simply failed to carry its burden, ordering disclosure outright rather than a remand for factfinding. Only the 2026 supreme court decision is cited here. Do not rely on the 2023 division opinion's statutory analysis.

People in Interest of My.K.M., 2022 CO 35, expressly OVERRULED People ex rel. K.D., 155 P.3d 634 (Colo. App. 2007), to the extent K.D. treated ICWA 'active efforts' as equivalent to 'reasonable efforts.' K.D. surfaced in searches and was deliberately excluded.

Two SCOTUS date_decided values were taken from the opinion record rather than the CourtListener cluster date_filed field, which is unreliable for older SCOTUS clusters: Santosky v. Kramer was decided March 24, 1982 (cluster date_filed shows 1982-02-22) and Lassiter was decided June 1, 1981 (cluster date_filed shows 1981-08-28, a later order date). Cluster ids, reporter citations and URLs are as returned by the API.
No unpublished or memorandum decisions were used. Every cluster fetched confirmed precedential_status = Published.

GAPS — nodes with no on-point published Colorado authority found after targeted searching of colo and coloctapp. (a) DEC-06 Differential/Alternative Response and ACT-01 Voluntary Services: Colorado has no published appellate decision construing its differential-response track or voluntary service agreements as such; the entries give the nearest Colorado authority on when service-based alternatives are and are not statutorily available (L.S., S.K., C.Z.), against the FFPSA/Title IV-B federal baseline. (b) OUT-04 Extended Foster Care / Aging Out: no published Colorado appellate decision construes Chafee or extended foster care to age 21; E.M. (continuing exclusive jurisdiction until majority) and R.S. (appealability of any final order) are the closest jurisdictional authority, and the federal baseline is Pub. L. 106-169 and Pub. L. 110-351. (c) FAIL-03 Federal Compliance Failure: no Colorado decision addresses CFSR penalties or Single Audit Act findings; the entries use ICWA and reasonable-efforts compliance cases as the nearest analogue. (d) PMC-01 through PMC-04 and PMC-06: CFSR monitoring, OIG/Single Audit review, CAPTA section 5106a(c) citizen review panels and the Protect Our Kids Act commission have generated no Colorado case law; those nodes carry the Colorado transparency and performance-standard decisions that make such oversight possible, plus the federal statutory baseline. (e) No Colorado appellate decision was found on children missing or absent from foster care.

ACT-05 (Protective Order) and ACT-06 (Emergency Medical/Psychological Care) each carry only two cases. S.L. v. District Court and Lovato v. District Court are the two controlling Colorado Supreme Court decisions on the juvenile court's pre-adjudicatory power to enter protective and medical orders under C.R.S. sections 19-1-104(3) and 19-2-103(5)(b) (now recodified in article 3 of title 19). Searches for more recent published Colorado authority on court-ordered medical treatment or exclusion orders in dependency returned nothing on point.

Section 1983 authority is Tenth Circuit, which is Colorado's circuit. Malik (Arapahoe County) and Doe v. Woodard (El Paso County) arise from Colorado county departments and are the most directly applicable; Gomes (Utah), Jones v. Hunt (New Mexico) and Dahn (Colorado placing officials, Oklahoma placement) bind Colorado district courts equally.

Practitioner caution on outcomes: Doe v. Woodard, Gomes and Dahn each ended in qualified immunity for the officials. They state the constitutional standard but did not produce liability. Malik and Jones v. Hunt are the two Tenth Circuit decisions in this set where qualified immunity was denied.

S.L. v. District Court (1984) and Lovato (1979) construe the pre-1987 Children's Code numbering (former sections 19-2-103, 19-3-111, 19-10-107). Their jurisdictional holdings remain good law but counsel must map them onto the current article 3 sections (19-3-401 to -405, -505, -508) before citing.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the CO node files are keyword-match noise with synthetic citations (In re People ex rel. J.D. appears in 70 files, In re Raykin and In re Marriage of Bailey are not child-welfare authority at all). Each candidate title was looked up; none survived retrieval and on-point review, so none was retained.

Colorado has no free-standing state ICWA statute; its implementation duties sit in C.R.S. section 19-1-126 (inquiry and notice), construed in People in Interest of A.D., with the substantive federal standards supplied by 25 U.S.C. sections 1912(d) and (f) as construed in My.K.M. and D.B.
Total CourtListener requests used: approximately 100 of the 150 budgeted, paced at one request per two seconds. No HTTP 429 was encountered. Justia was not fetched.
